learning_objective: 🎯 Explore how irrational hope and obsession can blind us to reality, through an old man who waits every single day for a 'tomorrow' that never comes!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Old Captain Hagberd lives in a small seaport town, stubbornly believing that his long-lost son Harry will return home 'tomorrow.' He has spent years furnishing a house and waiting for this imaginary day.

Bessie lives next door, enslaved as a caregiver to her abusive, blind father. She sympathizes with Hagberd and secretly shares his hope, dreaming that Harry's return might rescue her from her trapped life.
Harry actually returns—not as the dutiful son Hagberd imagined, but as a reckless, broke sailor looking for cash. He has no desire to settle down.
When Harry identifies himself, Captain Hagberd rejects him as an impostor because Harry arrived 'today,' and his true son is supposed to come 'tomorrow.' The obsession proves stronger than reality.

fun_activity.title: 📅 The 'Tomorrow' Trap
fun_activity.instructions: Have you ever put off a task saying 'I'll do it tomorrow' over and over? Write down one goal you have been postponing. Commit to doing just 5 minutes of it TODAY to break the Hagberd cycle!

exam_tips: 📌 Contrast the two fathers in the story: Captain Hagberd (delusional but gentle in his hope) and Josiah Carvil (blind, tyrannical, and bitter).
📌 Analyze the dramatic irony of the title 'Tomorrow': tomorrow is a word that constantly shifts and can never actually become present reality.
📌 Focus on Bessie's heartbreak at the end—she loses both the imaginary Harry and the real one, leaving her trapped forever.
quick_recap: ⭐ Captain Hagberd put advertisements in newspapers for years searching for Harry.
⭐ Harry ran away to sea sixteen years ago because of his father's strictness.
⭐ The old man's delusion protects him from grief, but completely destroys any chance of a real reconciliation.
